readings.title: The Skillful Huntsman, part 1: a bargain with the red stranger
readings.challenge: Watch a clever hero add a condition of his own to someone else’s bargain.
readings.focus: Jacob wants to marry the mayor’s daughter, and a stranger with a horse’s hoof offers to make him a perfect shot.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. Herr is German for Mister; a practical huntsman is one who really hunts; pottage is a thick soup; whithersoever means wherever. In old German tales a tall stranger in red with a horse’s hoof is the Devil in disguise.
readings.contentNote: Jacob signs a bargain with a stranger who is plainly the Devil of folktales; the story treats it as a contest of wits.

excerpt.locator: “The Skillful Huntsman,” from the start through Jacob signing the stranger’s paper; opens “Once upon a time there was a lad named Jacob Boehm, who was a practical huntsman.”; closes “…After that Jacob signed the paper, and the stranger went one way and he went home again.”.

questions.prompt: What must Jacob do before he may marry Gretchen? Why might the Herr Mayor set such a hard task?
facilitatorNotes: Shoot the whiskers off a running hare without touching its skin. It sounds impossible, so perhaps the mayor hopes Jacob will give up; Jacob’s mother expects the same.
evidence: shoot the whiskers off from a running hare without touching the skin
many a man wants and wants, and nothing comes of it!

questions.prompt: Jacob keeps saying the same thing. What is it, and what does it tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: “What one man has done, another man can.” He is stubborn and sure of himself; nothing his mother says will stop him.
evidence: what one man has done, another man can

questions.prompt: What clues tell Jacob, and you, that the stranger should not be trusted?
facilitatorNotes: He knows Jacob’s name without being told, he has a horse’s hoof instead of a foot, he wants a signature, and he makes a sour face at the word “condition.”
evidence: the stranger had a horse's hoof instead of a foot
as though he had sour beer in his mouth

questions.prompt: What is Jacob’s condition, and how might it save him?
facilitatorNotes: The stranger must be his servant for ten years, and if Jacob asks a question he cannot answer, Jacob goes free. It gives Jacob a way out; children can guess what kind of question might work.
evidence: if, in all that time, I should chance to ask you a question that you cannot answer, then I am to be my own man again

readings.title: The Skillful Huntsman, part 2: a plough and a purse
readings.challenge: Notice a pattern repeat, and decide what each new demand shows about the person making it.
readings.focus: The mayor keeps changing his demands, and the red servant supplies each wonder.
readings.context: Recap: to marry Gretchen, the Herr Mayor’s daughter, Jacob Boehm had to shoot the whiskers off a running hare. A tall stranger in red with a horse’s hoof made him a perfect shot, in return for Jacob’s promise to go with him in ten years, unless Jacob can ask him a question he cannot answer. Until then the stranger must serve Jacob and come when he blows a bone whistle. A magpie is a long-tailed bird; a furrow is a groove cut by a plough.

excerpt.locator: “The Skillful Huntsman,” from Jacob’s return to the Herr Mayor through his marriage to Gretchen; opens “Well, Jacob brushed the straws off from his coat, and put a fine shine on his boots, and…”; closes “…his Gretchen, and, between his plough and his purse, he was busy enough, I can tell you.”.

questions.prompt: Each time Jacob passes a test, what does the Herr Mayor do?
facilitatorNotes: He hems and haws, scratches his head, and names something new that he has “always said and sworn.” The repeated words suggest he is making it up as he goes.
evidence: At this the Herr Mayor scratched his head, and hemmed and hawed.
he had always said and sworn

questions.prompt: Where does Jacob go to call the red one, and how does the red one arrive?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the wood-pile. He appears at once, as if he had stepped out of “the door of nowheres,” Pyle’s funny way of saying out of thin air.
evidence: back of the wood-pile
as though he had just stepped out of the door of nowheres

questions.prompt: Why does the Herr Mayor finally say yes?
facilitatorNotes: Because a son-in-law with a purse that never empties is too good to refuse. Money, not Jacob’s shooting or ploughing, wins him over. Children can say what they think of the mayor.
evidence: who would not like to have a lad for a son-in-law who always had two pennies more in his purse than he could spend

questions.prompt: The storyteller breaks in: “hui! I would like to have such a purse as that.” Who is talking to us, and why put that in?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator himself, joking with the listeners, as if the tale were being told aloud by the fire. Ask whether the child would want such a purse.
evidence: hui! I would like to have such a purse as that.

readings.title: The Skillful Huntsman, part 3: Gretchen’s riddle
readings.challenge: Work out a trick before the story explains it.
readings.focus: Gretchen turns herself into a creature no one can name, and Jacob asks the question the red one cannot answer.
readings.context: Recap: the red stranger with a horse’s hoof made Jacob Boehm a perfect shot and, as his servant, gave him a plough that ploughs by itself and a purse that never empties, so that Jacob could marry Gretchen. Now the ten years are over, and Jacob must go with the red one unless he asks a question the red one cannot answer. In a sorry state of dumps means very gloomy; a wren is a tiny bird and a raven a large black one; a scrape is a fix or a trouble.

excerpt.locator: “The Skillful Huntsman,” from the end of the ten years to the end of the tale; opens “So the days went on and on and on until the ten years had gone by and the time had come…”; closes “…another man beside Jacob Boehm would find himself in a pretty scrape only for his wife.”.

questions.prompt: How does Gretchen find out what is troubling Jacob?
facilitatorNotes: She can see there is more than he says and keeps teasing until he tells her everything. He tried to hide it; she noticed.
evidence: she could see that there was more to be told than Jacob had spoken

questions.prompt: Why does Gretchen roll herself in honey and feathers?
facilitatorNotes: So that she looks like a great bird that is no bird anyone knows, and the red one cannot say what it is. Children may guess the plan before the story says it.
evidence: she looked just like a great bird

questions.prompt: Why won’t Jacob shoot at the wren or the raven?
facilitatorNotes: He makes excuses (too small, too black) because he is waiting for Gretchen. Each refusal makes the red one more impatient.
evidence: that is too small
that is too black

questions.prompt: The verse at the end gives the story’s meaning. Who is the real hero, Jacob or Gretchen?
facilitatorNotes: Pyle says many men would be in trouble without their wives. Jacob’s condition made escape possible, but Gretchen thought of how to use it. Children can argue for either, or both.
evidence: I can help you out of your trouble easily enough
in a pretty scrape only for his wife.

readings.title: Venturesome Boldness
readings.challenge: Compare a character setting out with the same character coming home.
readings.focus: A tailor proud of killing a mouse goes looking for someone as bold as himself, and meets a knight.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. Venturesome means daring; slew means killed; a Jack is a fellow; pardie is an old word meaning “indeed!”; a brand is a sword; awry means crooked; “gone to pie” means fallen to pieces; “of less degree” means of lower rank, or smaller.

excerpt.locator: “Venturesome Boldness,” the whole poem; opens “A tailor came a-walking by, The fire of courage in his eye. "Where are you going, sir?"…”; closes “…shall there remain. A little man, Sir, always can Be great with folk of less degree!"”.

questions.prompt: What brave deed is the tailor so proud of?
facilitatorNotes: He killed a mouse in the house where the tailors live. The joke is how proud he is of something so small.
evidence: I slew a mouse

questions.prompt: How has the tailor changed when he comes by the second time?
facilitatorNotes: He limps, his face is woeful, his clothes are crooked and his courage is gone. The first and third verses match: “came a-walking by” becomes “came a-limping by.”
evidence: The fire of courage in his eye.
The tailor came a-limping by

questions.prompt: What happened when the tailor challenged the knight?
facilitatorNotes: The knight did exactly as he was asked, stood and drew his sword, and treated the tailor “outrageously.” The tailor got what he asked for.
evidence: He straightaway did
And treated me outrageously.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the tailor take home? Is it the right one?
facilitatorNotes: That a little man can always seem great among people smaller than himself, so he will stay home. Children may say he should have learned not to boast; the poem’s joke is that he learned the wrong lesson.
evidence: So I shall get me home again,
Be great with folk of less degree!

readings.title: A Victim to Science
readings.challenge: Notice what the characters forget while they argue.
readings.focus: Two learned doctors argue over the best cure for a sick crow until it is too late.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. He spells this verse the old-fashioned way: “ye” means “the,” and letters are left out of words such as th’r (their) and h’re (here). Physicians are doctors; Concord is a town in Massachusetts; a tincture and a tonic are liquid medicines; lassitude and languor mean tiredness; incontinently, in old usage, means at once. The moral “is apparent” means it is obvious.
readings.contentNote: The sick crow dies while the doctors argue.

excerpt.locator: “A Victim to Science,” the whole poem with “Ye Moral”; opens “Th're were two wise physicians once, of glory and renown, Who went to take a little walk…”; closes “(_is apparent_.)”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem describe the two doctors at the start? Does the ending agree?
facilitatorNotes: “Very, very great and wise and learned.” By the end they have lost their tempers while their patient died, so the praise turns out to be teasing.
evidence: Oh! very, very great and wise and learned men were they,
Until they lost their tempers

questions.prompt: What does each doctor want to give the crow, and what does each say against the other’s cure?
facilitatorNotes: One has pills, which the other calls too violent; the other has a tincture or tonic, which the first calls too weak.
evidence: Your pills, sir, are too violent.
Your tonic is too weak.

questions.prompt: How can you tell from the way the lines are written that the doctors keep interrupting each other?
facilitatorNotes: Their sentences break off with dashes, and the next speaker starts before the last one finishes. Reading it aloud in two voices makes it clear.
evidence: Now, I have had occasion--
Permit me, sir, to speak.

questions.prompt: Pyle does not write out the moral; he only says it “is apparent.” What is the moral, in your own words?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps that arguing about the best way to help can stop anyone helping at all, or that wanting to be right can matter more than the patient. Accept any moral that fits what happens to the crow.
evidence: Ye Crow, not waiting for ye end, incontinently died.
is apparent

readings.title: Play & Earnest
readings.challenge: Hear how a poem’s sound changes when its mood changes.
readings.focus: A playful breeze accepts a tree’s invitation and grows into a storm that tears the tree down.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. In earnest means seriously, not in play. A lea is a meadow; a mad-cap is someone wild and reckless; in rout means scattered in confusion; a tempest is a violent storm; rent means tore; asunder means apart.

excerpt.locator: “Play & Earnest,” the whole poem; opens “Over dewy hill and lea Merrily Rushed a mad-cap breeze at play, And the daisies, like the…”; closes “…from its crown; Till, at last, it flung it down, Stripped, and bare, and torn asunder.”.

questions.prompt: What is the breeze like at the beginning? Which words show it?
facilitatorNotes: Merry and wild, at play; the daisies dance and twinkle like stars as it passes.
evidence: Rushed a mad-cap breeze at play,
Danced and twinkled in its way.

questions.prompt: Who invites the breeze to play, and how do the leaves greet it?
facilitatorNotes: The tree invites it, and the leaves shiver and quiver with delight. The very short lines tremble like leaves.
evidence: Will you come and have a play?
Then the leaves, with sudden shiver,

questions.prompt: How does the last verse sound different from the first two?
facilitatorNotes: Its lines are longer and its words are rough: flung, tossed, roared, groaned, rent. The dancing short lines are gone, just as the play is gone.
evidence: Till it roared, as though with thunder.
Stripped, and bare, and torn asunder.

questions.prompt: The title is “Play & Earnest.” What do you think Pyle wants us to notice about play?
facilitatorNotes: That play can turn serious or harmful when one player grows too strong or stops caring about the game. Some children will see it simply as a picture of a storm; both readings fit.
evidence: For it cared to play no longer.

readings.title: The Accident of Birth
readings.challenge: Explain a joke that turns into a serious question.
readings.focus: An absent-minded stork delivers a prince to a cobbler’s house, and no one can tell the difference.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. An old story told children that storks brought new babies; here Saint Nicholas sends them. A petition is a request; dinning means noisy repeating; a cobbler mends shoes; half a score is ten; quoth he means he said. Stultzenmannenkim is a made-up, comically long German-sounding name, and Fritz is a nickname for Friedrich. Pyle lettered this poem in old-fashioned spelling: “ye” means “the.”

excerpt.locator: “The Accident of Birth,” the whole poem; opens “ _Saint Nicholas_ used to send, so I am told, All new-born babes by storks, in days of…”; closes “…so? Also, perhaps, _I_ should be great, instead Of writing thus, to earn my daily bread.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Saint Nicholas finally send King Friedrich Max a baby?
facilitatorNotes: He is tired of hearing the same prayer every day. Even a saint, the poem jokes, grows weary of being asked.
evidence: For one grows weary when one always hears

questions.prompt: What mistake does Wilhelm Stork make, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He takes the baby to Fritz the cobbler instead of Fritz the king, because he is old and slow-witted and both men are called Fritz. The cobbler already has ten children.
evidence: So what does he but bear ye gift to Fritz
Ye cobbler, who had half a score of such.

questions.prompt: The baby goes from being first of all to the last. Was the baby himself any different?
facilitatorNotes: No; only the house he landed in changed. The last verse argues that if an experienced stork cannot tell a new-born prince from a cobbler’s baby, perhaps there is no difference to tell.
evidence: From new-born cobbler's somewhat hard to know,

questions.prompt: In the last two lines the poet thinks about himself. What is he joking about?
facilitatorNotes: That perhaps he, too, was meant to be great and was delivered to the wrong house, so now he must write for a living. Children may hear only the joke, or the serious idea that being born rich or poor is luck.
evidence: should be great, instead
to earn my daily bread.

readings.title: Hans Hecklemann’s Luck, part 1: no luck at all
readings.challenge: Follow a tricky argument about luck, and decide whether it makes sense.
readings.focus: Hans Hecklemann has no luck at all, neither good nor bad, and his wife Catherine wants him to do something about it.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. Luck is what happens to someone by chance, good or bad; in this story luck is also a little creature you can carry about. A farthing was the smallest coin; “as poor as charity” means very poor; indifferent here means neither good nor bad; “he never laid one penny on top of the other” means he could never save. Lawyers earn their living by talking, so the storyteller jokes that they carry their luck under their tongues.

excerpt.locator: “Hans Hecklemann’s Luck,” from the start to Hans deciding to visit the wise woman; opens “Hans Hecklemann had no luck at all. Now and then we hear folks say that they have no…”; closes “…shown her how poor her advice was, he took it. Many other men are like Hans Hecklemann.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the storyteller say people carry their luck? Where is his own luck right now?
facilitatorNotes: In pocket-books, in hats, on finger tips and, for lawyers, under their tongues. His own luck is sitting astride his pen as he writes, though he cannot see it.
evidence: some carry it in their pocket-books
Mine is at this moment sitting astride of my pen

questions.prompt: How can the storyteller be sure Hans has no luck at all, rather than bad luck? Follow his reasons.
facilitatorNotes: Hans always has enough to eat, so his luck is not bad; he never saves a penny, so it is not good; he has food and clothes enough, so it is not indifferent. If it is none of these, it must be no luck at all. It is a playful argument that sounds very logical.
evidence: so his luck was not indifferent
you see that it could have been no luck at all

questions.prompt: Catherine says, “Doing nothing puts no cabbage into the pot.” What does Hans answer, and whom do you agree with?
facilitatorNotes: “It takes none out.” Catherine means you must act to get more; Hans means doing nothing at least loses nothing. Both have a point, and the rest of the story will test it.
evidence: Doing nothing puts no cabbage into the pot
It takes none out

questions.prompt: Hans argues with Catherine and then does what she says. Why argue first? What does the storyteller think of that?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to show that he knows more than she does, even as he takes her advice. The storyteller teases him, and adds that many other men are the same.
evidence: After he had clearly shown her how poor her advice was, he took it.
Many other men are like Hans Hecklemann.

readings.title: Hans Hecklemann’s Luck, part 2: the wise woman and the beetle
readings.challenge: Notice good advice, and notice when someone does not take it.
readings.focus: The old wise woman tells Hans he is well enough off, then shows him where to find his lost luck, which turns out to be an ugly little imp.
readings.context: Recap: Hans Hecklemann has no luck at all, neither good nor bad, though his family always has just enough. His wife Catherine told him to ask the old wise woman in the wood where he lost it; he argued, then went. Hedgerows are rows of bushes along a field; the cuckoo is a bird whose call says its name; thence means from there; Kneitlingen is a town in the story. A stone cross by the road was a sign of the Christian faith, the “good sign” in this story. A manikin or an imp is a tiny man, here a wicked little spirit; betwixt means between.

excerpt.locator: “Hans Hecklemann’s Luck,” from Hans’s walk to the wise woman to catching his luck in the sack; opens “So, early the next morning, Hans jogged along to the old wise woman's cottage, while the…”; closes “That is what Hans Hecklemann's luck was like.”.

questions.prompt: What does the wise woman ask Hans, and what does she advise?
facilitatorNotes: Whether he has enough to eat, to drink and to wear, and is warm in winter. He says yes to all, so she tells him to leave well enough alone, because luck can give him nothing more and might take away what he has.
evidence: Then you had better leave well enough alone
And it might take away the good things that you already have

questions.prompt: Why does Hans still want his luck back?
facilitatorNotes: It might put money in his pocket, and he thinks he could make good out of it even if it is bad. The wise woman doubts it; she sees he is set in his own way.
evidence: But it might put money into my pocket
he only talked stiffness into his stubbornness

questions.prompt: Where did Hans lose his luck, and why has it stayed there for three years?
facilitatorNotes: On the overturned stone cross where three roads meet, coming home from the fair; his luck was evil, so it stuck to the good sign like a fly to butter and could not get away.
evidence: it stuck to the good sign, as all evil things of that kind must, like a fly to butter

questions.prompt: “That is what Hans Hecklemann’s luck was like.” What was it like? What does that warn you about the rest of the story?
facilitatorNotes: A little manikin as long as a thumb and as black as ink, kicking, screeching and rolling its red eyes: ugly and bad-tempered. Hans’s luck is bad luck, so getting it back may bring trouble, just as the wise woman warned.
evidence: as black as ink
it kicked and screeched and rolled its red eyes in a very ugly way

readings.title: Hans Hecklemann’s Luck, part 3: gold in the furrows
readings.challenge: Decide who wins a bargain, and test the story’s lesson.
readings.focus: Hans makes his luck promise him a gold coin at the end of every furrow he ploughs, and finds out what that costs.
readings.context: Recap: Hans Hecklemann lost his luck years ago. The old wise woman told him he was well enough off without it, but he insisted, so she sent him to an old stone cross, where he caught his luck: an ugly little black imp. He tied it up in a sack of goat’s hair. To bargain is to argue over what you will give and get; thalers and golden nobles were coins; a furrow is the long groove a plough cuts in a field; to tarry is to delay; haggard means thin and worn out; “gone the way of all men” means died; heirs are the people who receive what someone leaves when he dies.
readings.contentNote: Hans works his horses until they drop, and he dies without any joy of his gold.

excerpt.locator: “Hans Hecklemann’s Luck,” from Hans bargaining with his luck to the end and its moral; opens “So Hans having his luck secure in the little sack began to bargain with it. "What will…”; closes “…as one does cabbages--with money. That happiness is the only good luck after all!”.

questions.prompt: How does Hans make his luck give in?
facilitatorNotes: He drops the sack into the nasty pot of dish-scrapings that Catherine boils into soap, and every day asks what it will give him to be let out, until after a week or more it gives in.
evidence: into a nasty pot where Catherine cast the scrapings of the dishes
At last Hans's luck gave in.

questions.prompt: Why does Hans turn down a thousand thalers, and what does he ask for instead?
facilitatorNotes: Coins melt away like snow, as his father used to say. He asks for a golden noble at the end of every furrow he ploughs, a supply that will not run out.
evidence: They melt away like snow
a golden noble at the end of every furrow

questions.prompt: Hans grows rich. Why is he unhappy?
facilitatorNotes: He does nothing but plough from dawn to dark, thinks only of getting gold faster, tells no one, and grows thin and worn. He ploughs up gold but not happiness.
evidence: he did not turn up happiness in the furrows along with them
He told no one how rich he was growing

questions.prompt: The luck laughed that Hans had made “an ill bargain.” Was it right? Which of the four lessons at the end matters most to you?
facilitatorNotes: Yes: the bad luck stayed in his pocket all along, and the gold went to his heirs. Children can choose among the four lessons; many will pick “happiness is the only good luck,” and some will remember the wise woman’s advice to leave well enough alone.
evidence: you have made an ill bargain, Hans
That happiness is the only good luck after all!

readings.title: Farmer Griggs’s Boggart, part 1: a knock at the door
readings.challenge: Spot the moment a character makes a choice he will regret.
readings.focus: On a snowy night a tiny boggart knocks at Farmer Griggs’s door and promises to do all the work of the house if only he is let in.
readings.context: Howard Pyle, an American writer and artist, wrote and illustrated these tales and verses in the 1880s in the style of old German folktales and ballads; his pictures are not included here. A boggart is a mischievous house-imp from old English tales. The Griggses speak an old country dialect: “’ee” and “thee” mean you, “un” means him, “na” means no or not, “sarvice” is service, “intull” is into, and “gert” is great; an oaf is a clumsy fool; “Zooks” is an exclamation. A wight is a little creature; hay-ricks are haystacks; a dunce-cap was a pointed hat once put on a pupil who had not learned his lessons; a latticed window has criss-cross frames; a groat was a small coin; a scullion and a serving wench were kitchen servants.

excerpt.locator: “Farmer Griggs’s Boggart,” from the start to the boggart getting into the house; opens “Did you ever hear of a boggart? No! Then I will tell you. A boggart is a small imp that…”; closes “…such easy matter getting rid of the likes of him when we once let him in, I can tell you.”.

questions.prompt: What is a boggart, as the storyteller explains it, and what do we call such things now?
facilitatorNotes: A small imp that lives unseen in a house, doing a little good and much harm. Now we call them ill-temper, meanness, uncharitableness and the like, so the story may be about bad habits as well as imps.
evidence: doing a little good and much harm
ill-temper, meanness, uncharitableness, and the like

questions.prompt: How does Pyle make the farm-house feel cosy while the cold wind blows?
facilitatorNotes: Logs crackle in the wide chimney, Farmer Griggs warms his knees and his ale, the spinning-wheel hums like bees, the cat purrs and the dog basks. The cold outside makes the inside feel warmer.
evidence: But inside the farm-house all was warm and pleasant
like a whole hiveful of bees

questions.prompt: Farmer Griggs first says no. What changes his mind?
facilitatorNotes: The long list of chores the boggart promises to do, so that he need not pay any servants. The farmer and the dame both keep listening.
evidence: so that you will not have to give so much as a groat for wages
Then Farmer Griggs listened a little longer without shutting the door

questions.prompt: Dame Griggs calls only, “Shut the door!” How does the boggart end up inside, and who is to blame?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer shuts the door with the boggart already in. He hesitated, and she wanted the cold kept out. Children may blame the farmer, both of them, or the boggart’s clever promises; the storyteller warns that such a guest is hard to get rid of once you let him in.
evidence: Then Farmer Griggs shut the door, but the boggart was on the inside.

readings.title: Farmer Griggs’s Boggart, part 2: the boggart in the churn
readings.challenge: Explain why running away does not solve the problem in this story.
readings.focus: The boggart does all the work at first, then begins to play mean tricks, and when the family moves away to escape him, he comes too.
readings.context: Recap: on a snowy night a tiny boggart called Hardfist knocked at Farmer Georgie Griggs’s door and promised to do all the work of the house. The farmer hesitated, Dame Griggs called to him to shut the door against the cold, and the boggart ended up inside. In the Griggses’ dialect “’ee” and “thee” mean you, “un” means him, and “tull” or “intull” means to or into. Deftly means skilfully; pottage is porridge; rush-lights were cheap candles; to pilfer is to steal; magpies are birds said to steal; a coverlid is a bedcover; “Odds bodkins” and “Dang un!” are old exclamations; a wain is a big cart; bairns are children; fieldfares are birds that fly away each autumn; flittin’ means moving house; a churn is a tall tub for making butter.
readings.contentNote: The boggart starves the cat and dog, takes the children’s food and pulls off their covers at night; the farmer blames his wife for the trouble.

excerpt.locator: “Farmer Griggs’s Boggart,” from the boggart warming himself at the fire to the family’s return home; opens “The boggart came straightway over to the warm fire, and the dog…”; closes “…by going from here to there, for it is sure to be in the cart with the household things.”.

questions.prompt: Why can no one see the boggart once he is inside?
facilitatorNotes: Imps like him can be seen only as frost is seen, when it is cold; as he warmed by the fire he grew thin like a jelly-fish until he was like thin air.
evidence: can only be seen as the frost is seen--when it is cold

questions.prompt: At first everything goes “as smooth as cream.” What changes, and who suffers?
facilitatorNotes: Once he is comfortable he begins his pranks: scraping the butter so the farmer is jeered at market, skimming the children’s milk, starving the cat and the dog, blowing out the lights, chilling the fires and pulling the covers off the children.
evidence: mischief began to play the pipes and he began to show his pranks
he skimmed the children's milk

questions.prompt: Farmer Griggs blames his wife. What does the storyteller think of that? Is it fair?
facilitatorNotes: The storyteller says some men lay their own bundle of faults on their wives’ shoulders; the farmer let the boggart in himself. Dame Griggs answers that she told him only to shut the door.
evidence: lay their own bundle of faults on their wives' shoulders
I bade thee do naught but shut the door!

questions.prompt: Why do the Griggses go back to their old house? What does the storyteller want you to understand?
facilitatorNotes: The boggart was riding along in the churn, so moving would not help; better to bear trouble at home than in a new place. If the boggart stands for bad temper or meanness, you take it with you wherever you go.
evidence: for sure it's better to bear trouble there than in a new place
it is sure to be in the cart with the household things

readings.title: Farmer Griggs’s Boggart, part 3: a suit of clothes
readings.challenge: Work out why a present can make an unwanted guest leave.
readings.focus: The wise man Father Grimes tells Farmer Griggs how to be rid of his boggart, and it is not what you might expect.
readings.context: Recap: Farmer Griggs let a boggart into his house; it did the work at first but then played mean tricks on everyone. The family packed up to move away, but the boggart rode along in the butter churn, so they went home again. Breeches and breeks are trousers that end at the knee; shoen is an old word for shoes; “fitted like wax” means fitted perfectly; alackaday means alas. In old English tales a house-spirit given a present of clothes would leave and never come back.

excerpt.locator: “Farmer Griggs’s Boggart,” from the visit to Father Grimes to the end; opens “But how did Georgie Griggs get rid of his boggart? That I will tell you.”; closes “…left to us, like good Father Grimes, to tell one an easy way to get rid of one's boggart.”.

questions.prompt: What does Farmer Griggs have made, and where does he put the things?
facilitatorNotes: A red coat and blue breeches from Hugh the tailor, a velvet cap with a bell from William the hatter, and little shoes from Thomas the shoemaker. He lays them on the warm spot on the hearth where the boggart sleeps, and hides in the closet with his dame.
evidence: make a pretty red coat and a neat pair of blue breeches
He laid them on a warm spot on the hearth

questions.prompt: How does each piece of clothing fit the boggart?
facilitatorNotes: The hat fits exactly, the coat like wax, the breeches as though they grew there, and the shoes better than any shoes ever fitted. Every fit is perfect.
evidence: it fitted like wax
there never was such a fit

questions.prompt: Read the boggart’s song. Why does he say a house where he is given clothes cannot be his?
facilitatorNotes: Children may say he is too fine now to stay a servant, or that a gift means he has been paid off and must go; the song says the house of an honest man is not the place for him. Accept ideas the song supports.
evidence: If these be mine, mine cannot be
The house of honest man, Georgie!

questions.prompt: The storyteller says he has a boggart in his own house. What might he mean, and could he get rid of it so easily?
facilitatorNotes: Remember that boggarts stand for ill-temper and meanness: he means a bad habit of his own. He would dress it in silk and hang a silver bell on its cap, but there are no wise men left to tell an easy way. Children can talk about how people really chase away a grumpy mood or a mean habit.
evidence: for I have one in my own house
there are no more wise men left to us
